item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q007_chey_like_function_divergence","answer":"SCOPe supports a remote structural/evolutionary relationship at the CheY-like superfamily level: canonical CheY-related receiver domains, the N-terminal wing of ornithine decarboxylase, and the KaiA N-terminal domain all lie in the all-alpha/all-beta flavodoxin-like / CheY-like part of class c, but they are separated below that level into different families. The safe inference is therefore that these domains share the CheY-like receiver-domain fold and probably descend from a very ancient receiver-like ancestor. The unsafe transfers are the specific activities. A CheY-related response-regulator family assignment can support two-component phospho-signaling only when the receiver active-site features are present, especially the acidic pocket with the phosphorylatable Asp and the Mg2+-binding residues; those residues and that signaling chemistry should not be projected onto the KaiA N-terminal pseudo-receiver or onto the ornithine-decarboxylase wing just because SCOPe places the domains in the same CheY-like superfamily. Conversely, ornithine decarboxylation is a property of the full PLP-dependent ornithine decarboxylase architecture, not a generic property of CheY-like receiver domains or KaiA. KaiA’s N-terminal domain can be described as a CheY-like/pseudo-receiver domain in a cyanobacterial clock protein, but SCOPe co-classification does not by itself make it a phosphorylated CheY-like response regulator, an ornithine decarboxylase catalytic domain, or a template from which those functions should be transferred among the three family-level groups.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
